strengths: Well-motivated premise: addresses a recognized failure mode of multimodal in-context learning (ICL) in smaller LMMs, where long visual token contexts degrade induction and reasoning performance.

Comprehensive empirical analyses, including detailed breakdowns into task induction, perception, and reasoning components on the Operator Induction task, as well as sensitivity to prompt length and visual perturbations (e.g., CutMix, MixUp, Gaussian blur).
Clear structure and transparent experimental reporting, including hyperparameter configurations, test-time adaptation details, qualitative step-by-step predictions, and pseudo-code in the appendix.
weaknesses: Fairness and paradigm mismatch in comparison with ICL: ICL is strictly a feed-forward, training-free inference mechanism. Comparing ICL against test-time gradient-based adaptation (FT with up to 30 gradient descent steps) creates an uneven comparison in computational budget, latency, and memory requirements. Notably, when MAPD is evaluated purely under the inference-only ICL setting (Table 1, TTA = ICL), its advantages largely disappear and it is often outperformed by In-ContextPD.

Incremental technical novelty: The methodology combines existing ideas—specifically the attention-mapper architecture from Najdenkoska et al. (2023), soft prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021), and first-order MAML (Finn et al., 2017; Antoniou et al., 2019)—without introducing substantial algorithmic innovations to meta-learning or vision-language fusion.

Marginal improvement over standard multi-task baseline: The performance delta between MAPD and Multi-TaskPD under test-time finetuning is relatively narrow across several benchmarks (e.g., 77.9% vs. 74.6% on Open-MI, 47.7% vs. 45.1% on Operator Induction, 31.4% vs. 29.9% on CLEVR), raising questions as to whether the bi-level meta-optimization significantly outperforms standard multi-task pretraining followed by test-time fine-tuning.

Narrow benchmark scope: Evaluation is limited to four synthetic/semi-synthetic single-image tasks from the VL-ICL Bench. Evaluation on broader, realistic few-shot multimodal benchmarks (e.g., MMMU, MathVista, or standard fine-grained VQA) is needed to validate real-world applicability.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a well-known vulnerability of smaller (<7B) LMMs, which frequently fail to exhibit monotonic in-context learning gains due to long visual contexts.

The proposed architecture is parameter-efficient, replacing the standard MLP projection layer with a multi-head attention-mapper and learnable prompt tokens (amounting to only ~24M trainable parameters).

Comprehensive experimental analysis on the VL-ICL benchmark, including ablations on prompt sequence length, detailed breakdown of reasoning components (perception vs. induction vs. math reasoning), and robustness evaluations against various visual perturbations (e.g., CutMix, MixUp, Gaussian blur).
The paper is well structured, clearly written, and accompanied by detailed implementation descriptions and qualitative examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core comparison frames test-time gradient adaptation (FT) as an alternative to in-context learning (ICL). Because test-time finetuning involves full backpropagation, gradient updates, and significantly higher computational/latency overhead (~5x TFLOPs as shown in Appendix A.4), outperforming frozen forward-pass ICL is expected rather than surprising.

Marginal improvement over the simpler Multi-Task baseline: When comparing MAPD against Multi-TaskPD under identical test-time finetuning conditions (Table 1), the performance margins are relatively small across benchmarks (e.g., 77.9 vs 74.6 on Open-MI, 47.7 vs 45.1 on Operator Induction, 31.4 vs 29.9 on CLEVR Count), while FoMAML meta-learning introduces significant training complexity and doubles the wall-clock training time (10 hours vs 4.5 hours).

Questionable test-time validation protocol: In Section A.2.2, the authors note that they sample 10% of training data from each test task to form a validation set for early stopping and step selection ($K$). In realistic few-shot / test-time adaptation regimes, access to a separate validation split for each unseen downstream task is impractical and diverges from the standard few-shot setup.

Limited scope of evaluation: Evaluation is strictly restricted to single-image question answering tasks, despite multi-image interleaved contexts being one of the central paradigms of multimodal in-context learning.

Limited architectural novelty: The attention-based mapping mechanism is heavily inspired by Najdenkoska et al. (2023) and the meta-learning optimization utilizes standard first-order MAML (Antoniou et al., 2019), making the technical contribution largely an application of existing techniques to LLaVA/Qwen.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge: mitigating the brittleness and non-monotonic scaling of in-context learning (ICL) in moderate-sized Large Multimodal Models (LMMs).
The paper is well-organized, with comprehensive documentation in the appendix covering implementation details, hyperparameters, and qualitative prediction traces.

Provides thoughtful diagnostic ablations, such as decomposing the Operator Induction task into perception, task induction, and mathematical reasoning, as well as robustness evaluations under image corruptions.
weaknesses: Unfair / Asymmetrical Comparison between ICL and Test-Time Finetuning: The core claim contrasts MAPD's test-time finetuning (FT) against standard In-Context Learning (ICL). ICL is purely feedforward at inference time, whereas MAPD requires backpropagating through a 7B-parameter LLM for up to 30 gradient steps per task to update the mapper/prompt parameters. This introduces a substantial compute, memory, and latency footprint at test time (as noted in Appendix A.4), making direct comparisons against zero-training ICL problematic.

Marginal Gains over Standard Multi-Task Finetuning: When comparing MAPD + FT directly to Multi-TaskPD + FT (standard multi-task training without bi-level optimization, followed by test-time finetuning), the performance gains from MAML meta-learning are quite modest across benchmarks (e.g., 77.9% vs. 74.6% on Open-MI, 47.7% vs. 45.1% on Operator Induction, and 31.4% vs. 29.9% on CLEVR). This raises doubt about whether the complexity of first-order meta-learning provides significant practical benefits over straightforward multi-task tuning.

Limited Novelty: The conceptual and algorithmic contributions are largely incremental combinations of existing techniques. The attention-mapper design closely follows Najdenkoska et al. (2023), and the optimization uses off-the-shelf first-order MAML (Finn et al., 2017; Antoniou et al., 2019) applied to prompt tuning, which has already been explored in similar vision-language settings (e.g., Qin et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b).

Restricted Evaluation Scope and Stronger Pretrained Baselines: The evaluation is confined to four single-image subtasks from the VL-ICL benchmark. Standard few-shot vision-language benchmarks are omitted. Furthermore, Table 9 shows that models like LLaVA-OneVision-7B with standard ICL significantly outperform LAQ-7B + MAPD (FT) on TextOCR (42.3% vs. 26.4%) and CLEVR (34.9% vs. 31.4%), demonstrating that better-trained base models with forward-only ICL can readily surpass test-time finetuned prompts.

Questionable Test-Time Adaptation Validation Protocol: In Appendix A.2.2, the authors note that they sample 10% of the training split of each target evaluation dataset as a validation set to select the optimal inner-loop step K (up to 30 steps) and tune learning rates. In a realistic few-shot deployment setting, having access to an auxiliary validation set from the target distribution is generally unrealistic and undermines the strict few-shot premise.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a well-documented issue in multimodal in-context learning (ICL), where smaller and medium-sized LMMs struggle with sequence length bloat and extraneous image token noise.
Well-designed, parameter-efficient framework (MAPD) that integrates an attention-mapper connector with learnable soft prompts, optimized via first-order MAML (FoMAML) on only ~24M parameters.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on the VL-ICL benchmark across four distinct task types, testing scaling behavior up to 64 shots, various backbone architectures (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Vicuna-7B, Qwen3-8B, SigLIP), and relevant PEFT baselines (e.g., LoRA).

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analyses, including connector architecture ablations (MLP vs. attention mapper, with and without soft prompts), soft prompt length scaling, attention entropy measurements, image perturbation robustness, and FLOPs-matched inference trade-offs.
weaknesses: Practical deployment overhead: unlike standard ICL which requires only a single feedforward pass, MAPD relies on test-time gradient descent (up to 30 steps per task/query), introducing state management complexity and roughly doubling inference latency.

Incremental gains over Multi-Task baseline: while MAPD consistently outperforms Multi-TaskPD with test-time finetuning, the margin is often modest (e.g., 31.4% vs. 29.9% on CLEVR, 47.7% vs. 45.1% on Operator Induction, 26.4% vs. 22.9% on TextOCR), suggesting that a large portion of the gain comes from prompt distillation and connector finetuning rather than bi-level meta-optimization.
Scope is restricted to single-image VQA tasks, leaving multi-image and interleaved multimodal ICL scenarios unexplored.

Minor presentation omissions, such as an incomplete footnote on page 1 ('We release our code here -') and missing table reference text in Section A.1.2 ('alongside those listed in Table, performing').

strengths: Addresses an important and well-documented problem in multimodal learning: the degradation and instability of in-context learning (ICL) in smaller (≤7B) Large Multimodal Models (LMMs).

Parameter-efficient and modular design: updating only ~24M parameters (the attention mapper and soft prompts) while keeping the visual encoder and base LLM frozen makes meta-training feasible on moderate compute budgets.

Thorough empirical evaluation across several baselines (NoMeta-task, Model-Avg, In-Context, Multi-Task, and LoRA variants) and across multiple model architectures (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B, Vicuna, SigLIP, Qwen3-8B).

Extensive diagnostic and ablation analysis, including attention entropy analysis, FLOPs-matched test-time compute comparisons, subtask breakdowns on Operator Induction, and robustness to image perturbations.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: combining soft prompt tuning, cross-attention projection modules, and first-order MAML (FoMAML) builds closely on prior frameworks such as Najdenkoska et al. (2023) and standard prompt-tuning meta-learning literature.

Practical deployment limitations of test-time gradient adaptation: unlike feed-forward ICL, test-time adaptation requires calculating gradients and updating parameters for each new task/session, introducing non-trivial runtime overhead and engineering complexity in standard inference serving systems.
Evaluation scope is restricted to single-image VQA tasks from VL-ICL Bench; multi-image reasoning and broader multimodal benchmarks (e.g., MMMU, MathVista) are left out.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a known pathology: Smaller Large Multimodal Models (LMMs, $\le 7$B) frequently experience degradation or plateauing performance in multimodal in-context learning (ICL) due to long-context distraction and continuous image token bloat.

Parameter-efficient and modular architectural design: Integrating the Attention-Mapper into the projection layer and keeping the vision encoder and LLM frozen restricts the meta-learned and adapted parameters to only ~24M, enabling fast convergence during test-time adaptation (within $\le 30$ steps).

Extensive experimental evaluation and baselines: The paper benchmarks against a diverse array of baselines, including vanilla ICL, standard LoRA variants (across different layers and connector), multi-task prompt distillation, in-context prompt distillation, and model averaging across tasks from the VL-ICL Benchmark.

Thorough ablations and diagnostic analyses: The paper provides substantial supplementary analyses, including variations across vision encoders (SigLIP vs. CLIP) and LLM backbones (Qwen2.5-3B, Vicuna-1.5, Qwen3-8B), prompt length scaling, attention entropy calculations, robustness to visual perturbations (CutMix, MixUp, blurring), and subtask-level breakdown on operator induction.
weaknesses: Unbalanced comparison between test-time gradient adaptation and inference-only ICL: While the paper includes a FLOPs and latency discussion in Appendix A.3, comparing a gradient-based optimization method (requiring backward passes, memory for activations, and hyperparameter tuning of learning rates) directly against standard training-free ICL represents an asymmetry in operational assumptions and deployment constraints.

Incremental algorithmic novelty: The framework primarily combines First-Order MAML (FoMAML) with cross-attention connector / soft prompt distillation, both of which are well-established paradigms in meta-learning and vision-language tuning. The conceptual leap beyond existing meta-prompting literature (e.g., Najdenkoska et al., 2023) is moderate.

Modest margins over the multi-task baseline: The bi-level meta-optimization of MAPD brings relatively small improvements over the simpler single-level Multi-TaskPD baseline on several tasks (e.g., in Table 1, 31.4% vs. 29.9% on CLEVR, 47.7% vs. 45.1% on Operator Induction, and 77.9% vs. 74.6% on Open-MI), which raises questions regarding whether the computational overhead of meta-learning training is fully justified.

Evaluation restricted to single-image setups: Real-world multimodal ICL tasks frequently involve multiple images across context demonstrations. Restricting the evaluation exclusively to single-image tasks limits the demonstration of the approach's generalizability across more complex multimodal reasoning regimes.
